notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Acts 7:31–60, drawn from the sources specified. (I was unable to fetch pages from Catholic, Orthodox, or modern‑scholarship sites because of tool limits; those traditions are therefore noted where the sources I did read mention them, but I could not retrieve primary content from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, or netbible.org.)

---

**v. 31 — “When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight. As he approached to look more closely, the voice of the Lord came to him:”**

Gill notes that a bush on fire was not extraordinary, but a bush burning without being consumed “was wonderful indeed.” Moses’ wonder was stirred by the phenomenon before he knew the divine presence was in it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Gill’s Exposition)

Barnes adds that what “particularly attracted his attention was the fact that the bush was not consumed” (Ex. 3:2–3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Barnes’ Notes)

Calvin observes that God used such a wonder so that Moses “might assuredly know his majesty” and distinguish true revelation from “the juggling casts of Satan.” The marvel drew Moses near; then God spoke, confirming the divine origin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Calvin’s Commentary)

Matthew Henry remarks that Moses “had the curiosity at first to pry into it,” but the nearer he drew “the more he was struck with amazement.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Henry’s Complete)

---

**v. 32 — “ ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.’ Moses trembled with fear and did not dare to look.”**

Henry explains that God here declares the covenant made with Abraham ages before is “still in full force.” It also proves the future state (as Jesus later argued, Mt. 22:31–32): “Abraham is dead, and yet God is still his God, therefore Abraham is still alive.” Stephen, far from blaspheming Moses, was doing “the greatest honour imaginable to Moses” by highlighting this revelation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Henry’s Complete)

Calvin adds that Moses “trembled, and durst not behold” because he was now aware that this was not a mere fiery meteor but “the Angel of the covenant, the Son of God himself.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Calvin’s Commentary)

---

**v. 33 — “Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’ ”**

Henry notes that Stephen highlights this to check those who “prided themselves in the temple, that holy place, as if there were no communion to be had with God but there; whereas God met Moses … in a remote obscure place in the wilderness of Sinai.” God is not confined to places. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Henry’s Complete)

Enduring Word similarly stresses that Stephen’s recurring point is that God, His glory, and His work were never confined to the temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 34 — “I have indeed seen the oppression of My people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning and have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you back to Egypt.”**

Enduring Word says Stephen emphasised that God both called and commissioned Moses — and did so from outside the land, outside any temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

Constable notes that God “commanded Moses to return to Egypt as His instrument of deliverance for the Israelites. God revealed Himself and His Law outside the Holy Land.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Constable’s Notes)

---

**v. 35 — “This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush.”**

Ellicott observes that the word translated “redeemer” (Greek *lutrōtēs*) “is not found elsewhere in the New Testament, but is formed from the noun for ‘ransom’ … and appears to have been chosen to emphasise the parallelism which the speech indicates between Moses and the Christ.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:35)

Enduring Word: “Even though Israel had rejected Moses and his leadership, God appointed Moses with unmistakable signs.” The pattern is deliberate: Israel rejected Moses at his “first coming,” yet he remained God’s chosen deliverer — exactly as with Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 36 — “He led them out and performed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and for forty years in the wilderness.”**

Ellicott: “The two nouns are joined together … the first emphasising the wonder which the miracle produces … the latter, the fact that the miracle is a token or evidence of something beyond itself.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:36)

---

**v. 37 — “This is the same Moses who told the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’ ”**

Ellicott notes that “the parallelism previously suggested is now distinctly proclaimed, and shown to be a fulfilment of the prediction of Deuteronomy 18:18.” Peter had already applied these words to Jesus (Acts 3:22), so Stephen’s hearers would have caught the drift. Ellicott adds that at this point we may “reasonably think of the members of the Sanhedrin as catching the drift of his discourse, and showing signs of excitement.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:37)

---

**v. 38 — “He was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. And he received living words to pass on to us.”**

Ellicott explains “living oracles” (*lively oracles*, KJV) as words that are “not dead, but living, life-giving” — a striking description of the law as God’s living speech, not a dead code. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm)

---

**v. 39 — “But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt.”**

Enduring Word: Stephen draws the uncomfortable parallel — just as ancient Israel rejected Moses, so the present leaders are rejecting the Prophet like Moses. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 40 — “They said to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us! As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’ ”**

The quotation follows Exodus 32:1 closely. Stephen is building the case that Israel’s history is a repeated pattern of rejecting God’s messengers and turning to man-made religion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 41 — “At that time they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, rejoicing in the works of their hands.”**

Enduring Word draws the pointed application: “Just as Israel worshipped the calf in the wilderness, so now they were worshipping the works of their own hands” — the temple had become an idol. One of the charges against Stephen was blaspheming the temple, but he was really opposing the way Israel “worshipped the temple of God instead of the God of the temple.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 42 — “But God turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets:”**

Enduring Word: The phrase “God turned and gave them up” is both important and awesome. Paul later developed this thought in Romans 1:24–32. It prompts the question: “If we reject Jesus, what will we be given up to?” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 43 — “You have taken along the tabernacle of Molech and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.”**

Enduring Word notes that Stephen quotes Amos 5:25–27 but changes “beyond Damascus” to “beyond Babylon.” Boice explains this is because Stephen is addressing the leaders of the southern kingdom (Judah), not the northern kingdom as Amos was. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 44 — “Our fathers had the tabernacle of the Testimony with them in the wilderness. It was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen.”**

Stephen now turns to answer the charge of speaking against the temple (Acts 6:13). He affirms that the tabernacle was divinely given and made according to the heavenly pattern — yet it was a tent, portable, not a permanent structure. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 45 — “And our fathers who received it brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations God drove out before them. It remained until the time of David,”**

Constable summarises that in this section (vv. 44–50) Stephen “deals with the temple and responds to the charge of speaking against the temple … and saying that Jesus would destroy the temple and alter Jewish customs.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-31.html, Constable’s Notes)

---

**v. 46 — “…who found favor in the sight of God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.”**

David’s desire to build a house for God is presented positively — yet even David was not permitted to build it. The timing and the builder were God’s choice, not man’s. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 47 — “But it was Solomon who built the house for Him.”**

The temple was Solomon’s work, not David’s. Stephen’s rapid movement from David to Solomon shows that the temple was a relatively late development in Israel’s history — God had been dwelling with His people long before any stone temple existed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 48 — “However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says:”**

Enduring Word: “Stephen confronted their idolatry of the temple. In doing so, they tried to confine God within the temple. Yet God is too big to fit in any temple man could make.” Guzik applies this to Christians who confine God to a church building: “the only place they meet God is at the church.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

Ellicott notes the parallel with Paul’s later Athenian address (Acts 17:24), suggesting Paul may have absorbed Stephen’s theology. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:48)

---

**v. 49 — “ ‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be?’ ”**

The quotation is from Isaiah 66:1–2. Stephen uses it to show that the Old Testament itself testifies that God cannot be housed in any building made by human hands. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 50 — “ ‘Has not My hand made all these things?’ ”**

The Creator of all things needs nothing from human builders. The verse completes the Isaiah citation and drives home Stephen’s point about the relativity of the temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 51 — “You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did.”**

Enduring Word: Stephen “takes the sharp knife of the Word and rips up the sins of the people” (quoting Spurgeon). “Stiff-necked” recalls Israel’s description in Exodus 32:9 and is used nearly 20 times in the OT. “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” draws from Jeremiah 9:26 and Deuteronomy 10:16. Essentially Stephen says, “You are just like the Gentiles in your rejection of the Lord.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

Spurgeon remarks, “He could not have delivered that searching address with greater fearlessness had he been assured that they would thank him for the operation; the fact that his death was certain had no other effect upon him than to make him yet more zealous.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 52 — “Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. And now you are His betrayers and murderers—”**

Stephen’s accusation reaches its climax: the Sanhedrin stands in direct continuity with their fathers who persecuted and killed the prophets. “The Righteous One” is a messianic title. They have now become betrayers and murderers of the One all the prophets pointed toward. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 53 — “you who received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it.”**

Ellicott notes a “remarkable parallelism between the speech and [Paul’s] later teaching,” citing the parallel with Galatians 3:19 (the law was “ordained through angels”). This is one piece of evidence that Paul, present at Stephen’s death, absorbed elements of Stephen’s thought. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:1–2)

Enduring Word: “This accusation must have outraged the members of the council. They prided themselves on their obedience to the law,” yet Stephen says they have not kept it — the ultimate insult to men who thought themselves “blameless” regarding the law (cf. Phil. 3:6). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 54 — “On hearing this, the members of the Sanhedrin were enraged, and they gnashed their teeth at him.”**

Ellicott translates “cut to the heart” (KJV) as literally “sawn through and through” — “a keener pang than the ‘pricked’ of Acts 2:37, producing, not repentance, but the frenzy of furious anger.” The gnashing of teeth is “the only example of the literal use of a phrase with which we are so familiar in its figurative application (Mt. 8:12; 13:42, etc.). Here it clearly expresses brute passion rather than despair.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:54)

---

**v. 55 — “But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.”**

Ellicott: “Being full of the Holy Ghost” (Greek *plērēs*) “implies, not a sudden inspiration, but a permanent state.” Stephen “had begun with speaking of ‘the God of glory’ (Acts 7:2). He ends with the vision of that glory as belonging to the Son of Man.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:55)

Why is Jesus *standing* rather than *sitting* (the usual posture, e.g., Mt. 26:64; Col. 3:1; Heb. 1:3)?

- **Ellicott**: Jesus stood “in the attitude of one who rises to help and welcome a follower who had shown himself faithful even unto death.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: “Sitting … is the usual attitude ascribed to our Lord in token of his victorious rest … Here he is seen standing, as rising to welcome his faithful martyr, and to place on his head the crown of life (Rev. 2:10).” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/7.htm)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: “Clearly, to express the eager interest with which He watched from the skies the scene in that council chamber, and the full tide of His Spirit which He was at that moment engaged in pouring into the heart of His heroical witness.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-55.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Jesus stood “in solidarity with Stephen at this moment of crisis.” Guzik also suggests Jesus may have been giving “a standing ovation” to the first martyr, or pleading Stephen’s case before the Father (Mt. 10:32). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)
- **Constable**: “Stephen has been confessing Christ before men, and now he sees Christ confessing His servant before God.” Jesus as “witness” and “advocate” — standing as the proper posture for a witness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-55.html)

The Pulpit Commentary further notes that the vision was given “to the inward spiritual eye, and not to that of sense. No priest or scribe saw the glory of the opened heavens.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/7.htm)

---

**v. 56 — “ ‘Look,’ he said, ‘I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.’ ”**

Ellicott observes that “Son of Man” appears here “only here outside the Gospels, and never in the Epistles … a noteworthy indication of the primitive date and truthfulness of the expression and the report.” Stephen uses the very title Jesus used of Himself before this same council (Mt. 26:64). The Sanhedrin would immediately recognise the echo — and the implication that the crucified Nazarene is now vindicated in heaven. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-55.htm)

Enduring Word: When Jesus declared before this same body that He would sit at God’s right hand, they condemned Him for blasphemy (Mt. 26:64–66). Now Stephen says he sees exactly that — and the council’s reaction is identical. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 57 — “At this they covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him.”**

Ellicott: “They stopped their ears” — they could not bear what they regarded as the culminating blasphemy. They “ran upon him with one accord” — the same unanimity with which the believers were of “one accord” in prayer (Acts 1:14); the Sanhedrin is united in murderous rage. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:57)

---

**v. 58 — “They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.”**

The stoning occurred outside the city, in accordance with Leviticus 24:14. The witnesses (required by Deut. 17:7 to cast the first stones) laid their outer garments at Saul’s feet — indicating Saul’s prominent role in overseeing the execution.

Enduring Word notes this is the first mention of Saul (Paul) in Scripture. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

---

**v. 59 — “While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.’ ”**

Ellicott calls these words “memorable as an instance of direct prayer addressed, to use the words of Pliny in reporting what he had learned of the worship of Christians, ‘to Christ as God’ (Epist. x. 97).” Stephen “could not think of Him whom he saw at the right hand of God, but as of One sharing the glory of the Father, hearing and answering prayer.” He notes the echo of Jesus’ own words: “The Son commended His Spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46); the disciple, in his turn, commends his spirit to the Son.” The word “God” in the KJV phrase “calling upon God” is in italics — an insertion; the original simply says “invoking.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:59)

The Pulpit Commentary: “The request, Receive my spirit, was a striking acknowledgment of the divinity of Christ. Only he who gave the spirit could receive it back again.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/7.htm)

Benson’s Commentary: “Surely such a solemn prayer addressed to him, in which a departing soul was thus committed into his hands, was such an act of worship as no good man could have paid to a mere creature; Stephen here worshipping Christ in the very same manner in which Christ worshipped the Father on the cross.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/acts-7.html)

Bible.org: “Stephen believed that he was going to heaven to be with Jesus (cf. 2 Cor. 5:6, 8) and not to hades.” (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)

---

**v. 60 — “Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them.’ And when he had said this, he fell asleep.”**

Ellicott: “The resemblance to the prayer of Christ, ‘Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do’ (Luke 23:34), could hardly have been accidental.” He adds the famous words of Augustine (Serm. 314–318): “We owe the conversion of Saul to the prayers of Stephen,” or in the Latin form quoted by the Pulpit Commentary: *“Si Stephanus non orasset, Ecclesia Paulum non haberet”* — “If Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm, Ellicott on Acts 7:60; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/7.htm)

Spurgeon develops this: “That blessed petition must have rankled in his heart … in after years he must have looked upon Stephen as being, if anyone was, his spiritual father, by whose dying prayer he was begotten unto God.” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/stephens-martyrdom)

Benson’s Commentary notes the Greek expression *mē stēsēs autois tēn hamartian* is literally “weigh not out to them this sin” — i.e., a punishment proportionable to it — alluding to passages where God is represented as weighing men’s deeds in the balances of justice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/acts-7.html)

The phrase “he fell asleep” is the consistent New Testament metaphor for the death of a believer (cf. John 11:11; 1 Thess. 4:13–14). The Pulpit Commentary: “Blessed rest after life’s toilsome day! Blessed contrast with the tumult of passion and violence which brought him down to the grave!” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/7.htm)

Spurgeon: “Calmly on the bosom of his God he has laid his head, and left his troubles for his God to bear.” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/stephens-martyrdom)

---

## Points Where Traditions Diverge

**Jesus “standing” (v. 55):** All the Protestant sources I read agree on the significance — Jesus rises to welcome, advocate for, or honour His martyr. No major denominational split emerged in the pages consulted; the difference is one of nuance, not doctrine. The Reformed commentator Calvin, however, is cautious: “For mine own part, I think that though these speeches be diverse, yet they signify both one thing. For neither sitting, nor yet standing, noteth out how the body of Christ was framed; but this is referred unto his power and kingdom.” (https://www.ccel.org/study/Acts_7:55-59)

**Stephen’s prayer to Jesus (v. 59):** All traditions represented in the sources read this as evidence of Christ’s divinity. Gill (Baptist/Calvinist), Ellicott (Anglican), the Pulpit Commentary (broadly Protestant), Benson (Methodist), and Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic) all treat Stephen’s direct address to Jesus as worship due to God alone. No source consulted disputed this.

**The law “ordained by angels” (v. 53):** Ellicott and Constable note the link to Galatians 3:19, where Paul says the law was “ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.” This is a point where Reformed and Baptist covenant theology sees the law as mediated (and therefore inferior to the direct promise given to Abraham), but the sources I read did not develop distinct denominational positions at length.

**Catholic and Orthodox views:** I was unable to retrieve pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org due to tool limits. The Pulpit Commentary, however, quotes St. Augustine’s sermons on St. Stephen’s feast day, indicating that the early and medieval Church held Stephen in high honour as the first martyr (proto-martyr) and saw his prayer as instrumental in Saul’s conversion. Augustine’s statement that “without Stephen’s prayer, the Church would not have had Paul” is widely cited across traditions.

---
